title: Growth Charts: Why the Curve Beats the Number
hook: A percentile compares your child to other kids the same age and sex — it's not a grade. The 10th is no better or worse than the 90th; what matters is the trend along your child's own curve.
key_points: A percentile is a comparison, not a score: 30th percentile means taller/heavier than 30% of peers — not a problem by itself.
The trend over time along your child's own curve matters far more than any single measurement.
Roughly the 3rd to 97th percentile is considered a normal range.
For birth to 24 months, providers use WHO charts (tracking weight, length, and head circumference), then switch to CDC charts after age 2.
content_html: It's easy to read a growth chart like a report card, but a percentile is just a comparison. If your child is at the 30th percentile for weight, they weigh more than 30% of kids the same age and sex and less than the other 70% — that's it. As the AAP explains, the 10th percentile is no better or worse than the 90th; for growth, we hope for consistency rather than a high number. Roughly the 3rd to 97th percentile is considered a normal range.
extra_html: What your pediatrician actually watches is the rate and trend of growth — how your child moves along their own curve across several visits. One isolated dot doesn't say much; the pattern over time does. For babies from birth to 24 months, providers use the WHO growth charts and track weight, length, and head circumference (head size is a window into brain growth in infancy), then switch to the CDC charts after age 2. This is general educational information from the AAP — if a measurement or trend ever looks off, that's a normal and worthwhile conversation to have with your pediatrician.

source.name: HealthyChildren.org (AAP) — Understanding Growth Charts: Percentiles & Z-Scores

related.title: Well-Child Visits: Your Regular Check-Ups
related.hook: Well-child visits aren't just for when something's wrong — they track growth and development, deliver vaccines on schedule, and catch problems early, even when your child seems perfectly fine.

related.title: Developmental Milestones: The Big Picture
related.hook: Development happens across several areas at once — social, language, thinking, and movement — and milestones describe what most kids do by an age, not deadlines every child must hit.

flashcards.prompt: What matters most when reading your child's growth chart?

choices.text: The trend along the child's own curve over time
A single measurement at one visit

flashcards.explanation_html: Percentiles compare a child to peers, not a grade to maximize. Consistency and the trend over multiple visits matter more than any one number.

flashcards.prompt: Which growth charts are used from birth to 24 months, and what do they track?
flashcards.back_html: The WHO charts are used for birth to 24 months, tracking weight, length, and head circumference. After age 2, providers switch to the CDC charts.
